title: Chapter 105 — Does the Whale’s Magnitude Diminish?—Will He Perish?
paragraphs: Inasmuch, then, as this Leviathan comes floundering down upon us from the headwaters of the Eternities, it may be fitly inquired whether, in the long course of his generations, he has not shrunk from the original bulk of his ancestors.

But upon investigation we find that not only are the whales of the present day superior in size to those whose fossil remains are found in the Tertiary system — embracing a distinct geological period prior to man — but of the whales found in that Tertiary system, those belonging to its later formations exceed in size those of its earlier ones.

Of all the pre-human whales yet unearthed, by far the largest is the Alabama one mentioned in the last chapter, and that was less than seventy feet long in the skeleton. Whereas, we have already seen, the tape-measure gives seventy-two feet for the skeleton of a large modern whale. And I have heard, on whalemen's authority, that sperm whales have been captured near a hundred feet long at the time of capture.
But may it not be that while the whales of the present hour are an advance in size upon those of all previous geological periods, they have degenerated since Adam's time?

Assuredly, we must think so, if we are to credit the accounts of such gentlemen as Pliny and the ancient naturalists generally. For Pliny tells us of whales that embraced acres of living bulk, and Aldrovandus of others which measured eight hundred feet in length — ropewalks and Thames Tunnels of whales! And even in the days of Banks and Solander, Cook's naturalists, we find a Danish member of the Academy of Sciences recording certain Icelandic whales at one hundred and twenty yards — that is, three hundred and sixty feet. And Lacepede, the French naturalist, in his elaborate history of whales, at the very beginning of his work, sets down the right whale at one hundred meters, three hundred and twenty-eight feet. And this work was published as late as 1825.

But will any whaleman believe these stories? No. The whale of today is as big as his ancestors in Pliny's time. And if ever I go where Pliny is, I, a whaleman — more of one than he was — will make bold to tell him so. Because I cannot understand how it is that while the Egyptian mummies buried thousands of years before even Pliny was born do not measure as much in their coffins as a modern Kentuckian in his socks, and while the cattle sculptured on the oldest Egyptian and Nineveh tablets plainly prove that the prize cattle of Smithfield not only equal but far exceed in size the fattest of Pharaoh's fat cows — in the face of all this, I will not admit that of all animals the whale alone should have shrunk.

But still another inquiry remains — one often debated by the more thoughtful Nantucketers. Whether, owing to the almost all-seeing lookouts at the mastheads of whale-ships now penetrating even through Bering Strait and into the remotest secret corners of the world, and the thousand harpoons and lances hurled along all continental coasts, the burning question is whether Leviathan can long endure so wide a chase and so remorseless a slaughter — whether he must not at last be exterminated from the waters, and the last whale, like the last man, smoke his last pipe and then himself evaporate in the final puff.

Comparing the humped herds of whales with the humped herds of buffalo which, not forty years ago, spread by the tens of thousands over the prairies of Illinois and Missouri, and shook their iron manes upon the sites of populous river-capitals where now the polite broker sells you land at a dollar an inch — in such a comparison, an irresistible argument would seem furnished to show that the hunted whale cannot now escape speedy extinction.

But you must look at this matter from every angle. Though so short a period ago — not a good lifetime — the census of the buffalo in Illinois exceeded the census of men now in London, and though at the present day not one horn or hoof of them remains in all that region, and though the cause of this wondrous extermination was the spear of man — yet the far different nature of the whale-hunt absolutely forbids so inglorious an end to the Leviathan. Forty men in one ship hunting sperm whales for forty-eight months think they have done extremely well, and thank God, if at last they carry home the oil of forty fish. Whereas, in the days of the old Canadian and Indian hunters and trappers of the West, when the far west was a wilderness and a virgin, the same number of men on horse for the same number of months would have slain not forty but forty thousand and more buffaloes — a fact that, if need were, could be statistically demonstrated.

Nor, considered rightly, does it seem any argument in favor of the gradual extinction of the sperm whale that in former years these Leviathans, in small pods, were encountered much more often than at present, and that in consequence the voyages were shorter and much more profitable. Because, as has been elsewhere noted, those whales, influenced by some instinct toward safety, now swim the seas in immense caravans, so that the scattered loners, pairs, and pods of other days are now gathered into vast but widely separated, infrequent armies. That is all. And equally false seems the notion that because the baleen whales no longer haunt many grounds where they formerly abounded, that species too is declining. For they are only being driven from promontory to cape; and if one coast is no longer enlivened with their spouts, then, be sure, some other and remoter shore has been very recently startled by the unfamiliar spectacle.

Furthermore: concerning these last-mentioned Leviathans, they have two firm fortresses which, in all human probability, will forever remain impregnable. And as upon the invasion of their valleys the frosty Swiss have retreated to their mountains, so, hunted from the open and sheltered seas, the baleen whales can at last resort to their polar citadels, and diving under the ultimate glassy barriers and walls there, come up among icy fields and floes — and in a charmed circle of everlasting December, bid defiance to all pursuit from man.

But as perhaps fifty of these baleen whales are harpooned for one sperm whale, some philosophers of the forecastle have concluded that this positive slaughter has already very seriously reduced their numbers. But though for some time past a number of these whales, not less than 13,000, have been annually killed on the northwest coast by the Americans alone, there are considerations which render even this circumstance of little account as a counterargument.

Natural as it is to be somewhat skeptical concerning the abundance of the more enormous creatures of the globe, yet what shall we say to Harto, the historian of Goa, when he tells us that at one hunt the King of Siam took 4,000 elephants; that in those regions elephants are as numerous as droves of cattle in temperate climates? And there seems no reason to doubt that if these elephants, which have now been hunted for thousands of years by Semiramis, by Porus, by Hannibal, and by all the successive monarchs of the East — if they still survive there in great numbers, how much more may the great whale outlast all hunting, since he has a pasture to roam in that is precisely twice as large as all Asia, both Americas, Europe and Africa, Australia, and all the islands of the sea combined.

Moreover: we are to consider that from the presumed great longevity of whales — their probably attaining the age of a century and more — at any one period of time, several distinct adult generations must be alive simultaneously. And what that means, we may gain some idea of by imagining all the graveyards, cemeteries, and family vaults of creation yielding up the live bodies of all the men, women, and children who were alive seventy-five years ago, and adding this countless host to the present human population of the globe.

Wherefore, for all these things, we account the whale immortal in his species, however perishable in his individual life. He swam the seas before the continents broke water; he once swam over the site of the Tuileries, and Windsor Castle, and the Kremlin. In Noah's flood he despised Noah's Ark; and if ever the world is to be flooded again, like the Netherlands, to kill off its rats, then the eternal whale will still survive, and rearing upon the topmost crest of the equatorial flood, spout his frothed defiance to the skies.
